Explain what a Gaussian pyramid is, how it is built, and why it only needs about 33% more storage than the original image.
risposta: A Gaussian pyramid is a multi-resolution representation where each level is built by Gaussian-filtering and downsampling the previous level by a factor of 2, giving progressively smaller, blurrier images useful for coarse-to-fine search. Higher levels lose high-frequency detail while keeping low-frequency/uniform regions. Since halving width and height gives 1/4 the pixels per level, the total is N + N/4 + N/16 + ... = N/(1-1/4) = 4/3 N, i.e. only ~33% more storage than the original.

domanda: Describe the Laplacian pyramid: how it is constructed, why it is lossless, and how the original is reconstructed.
risposta: The Laplacian pyramid stores the high-frequency residuals lost between Gaussian levels, making it lossless. Define REDUCE (blur+downsample) and EXPAND (upsample+blur). Each residual is Li = Gi - EXPAND(G(i+1)): the actual higher-resolution image minus the prediction from the coarser level. The full representation is all residuals {L0..L(n-1)} plus the smallest Gaussian level Gn. To reconstruct, start from Gn and for i from n-1 down to 0 compute Gi = EXPAND(G(i+1)) + Li, recovering G0 exactly. The residuals are called Laplacian because image-minus-blurred (a Difference of Gaussians) approximates the LoG operator.

domanda: Explain the pyramid blending algorithm and why it produces seamless results.
risposta: To blend two images A and B with a mask M: (1) build Laplacian pyramids LA and LB for the sources; (2) build a Gaussian pyramid GM for the mask, whose 0-1 values act as smooth blending weights at each scale; (3) at each level j form LCj = GMj*LAj + (1-GMj)*LBj; (4) collapse the combined Laplacian pyramid to get the output. Because blending happens per frequency band with a smoothly-varying mask, low frequencies blend over a wide region and high frequencies over a narrow one, avoiding the sharp seam of a simple cut-and-paste.
